cells.tense: You are here, at the edge of what is arriving, with the pen in your hand.
cells.act: let the path show itself instead of forcing clarity
cells.ask: Take the step the moment is offering, then wait. The next one shows up when it shows up.
cells.core:
Something is arriving, and you don't have to see the whole road to meet it. Direction is coming from what you actually feel, not from a plan you're forcing. When a feeling has really finished — not swallowed, finished — it turns into movement, and that movement is worth trusting. The way forward tends to show itself a step at a time when you stop demanding the route in advance. You can do the next thing before you've worked out the thing after it. That isn't recklessness. It's moving from what's already settled in you. You'll notice the difference in your body: the pushing has a grip to it, and the step doesn't.

The step is enough. What comes after it comes at its own pace, and you don't have to hurry it along.
cells.sheetLine: You can head somewhere without seeing the whole road.
cells.verb: moving with direction toward what you're headed for
cells.place: the threshold where what's outside is arriving now

cells.tense: You will have driven past the place you were heading before you notice you missed the turn.
cells.act: adjust one dial a little, then stop
cells.ask: Ease off the push you're hardest at, a small notch, and stop there. Nothing follows it.
cells.core:
You are moving hard, and the motion has stopped being yours to aim. That's the shape of it — the engine keeps running past the destination, and the next thing is already loaded before you arrive at this one. Feelings get overtaken before they've landed. This isn't weakness. It's momentum you built, doing what momentum does when nobody's touching the dial. A dial is exactly what it is: one small adjustment, made early, usually holds better than a big correction made late.

So ease off one push, just a notch, and stop there. The point isn't to slow everything down. It's to find out that you can touch the throttle without slamming it, and that nothing catastrophic happens when you don't.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving so fast you miss your own arrivals.
cells.verb: moving with direction toward what you're headed for
cells.place: the threshold where what's outside is arriving now

cells.tense: You were at that door and you are still standing at it.
cells.act: let the thing end that is already over
cells.ask: Practice leaving one finished thing alone. When you reach to reopen it, don't. Repeat as often as it takes.
cells.core:
There's a pull toward something, and you stay where you are. The pull is real; the step isn't happening. From the outside it looks like nothing, but what's actually going on is a door you're standing in front of without going through. Some of that is old: something didn't end when it ended, and the not-ending is what's keeping the feet still. That's the honest picture, and it isn't a character flaw. It's an unfinished piece.

The way out isn't effort pushed at the stuck place — pressure there just makes the standing heavier. It's finishing what's already done. Letting one finished thing be finished clears the floor at the door, and the step tends to become obvious once the floor is clear.
cells.sheetLine: There's a pull and your feet haven't moved.
cells.verb: moving with direction toward what you're headed for
cells.place: the threshold where what's outside is arriving now

cells.tense: You are already moving, or already stopped, and you would not say either one out loud.
cells.act: stand in the gap it leaves without rebuilding yet
cells.ask: Notice a habit as you do it, and just stand in the gap after. No length, no plan, no filling it in.
cells.core:
There's momentum in you that you don't count as yours. Either you're headed somewhere and telling yourself it's just how things go, or you're held in place and calling it life. Both are the same thing: the steering is happening without being owned. You can probably hear it in how you describe a week — everything happening to you, nothing quite chosen. That isn't a failure of character. It's the wrong person credited with the driving.

It won't be fixed by deciding to be different. It gets fixed by catching one small habit in the act and standing in the gap it leaves — no replacement, no plan, no verdict. The gap is where you find out you were the one doing it.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving or stopped, and calling it neither.
cells.verb: moving with direction toward what you're headed for

attempts.check: The draft's weakest claim is the Unacknowledged cell's 'or stagnation you can't see' — the record offers both faces, but a reader who is genuinely moving fast will hear only one and may reject the other as not-them; I lead with momentum-hiding and carry stagnation as the second face so either reader has a door. The ask — stand in the gap without rebuilding — survives being wrong: if nothing came down, the gap is a habit they can still stand in for a week, and it costs nothing but the urge to fix. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the Too Little handle 'behind you' — it's a good line, but it accuses; I keep the scene and drop the sting.

attempts.check: The four fixes are structural rather than cosmetic: the asks had all become 'do one bounded thing for a set period', so I've spread the shapes — one step taken, one small correction with a stop built in, one plain statement of something ended, one noticing left alone. The unsupported claim was never the mechanism but my habit of certifying the person ('you already know'), so each core now describes what is happening in a moment they could recognise and leaves the recognition to them. The ask survives being wrong in every cell — none of them requires believing the reading, only doing a small thing that a camera could see. The line that served the writer more than the person was the Too Much sheet line; it admired its own phrasing, so it is plainer now.
